content_voiceover: This slide gives you the International Neuroblastoma Risk Group, or I N R G, staging system, which is the modern staging approach based on imaging rather than surgical findings. Stage L one is a locoregional tumor without image-defined risk factors, so it's surgically resectable up front. Stage L two is a locoregional tumor that does have one or more image-defined risk factors, meaning it's touching or encasing critical structures and isn't safely resectable initially. Stage M is distant metastatic disease, excluding the special M-S category. And M-S, the special stage, is an L one or L two tumor with metastatic disease confined only to skin, liver, and or bone marrow, without other distant spread. Below that, the slide reminds you of the classic Stage 4-S definition from the older I N S S system, which board exams still like to test, an infant under one year old with a localized primary tumor, stage one, two-A, or two-B, that has spread only to skin, liver, and or bone marrow, and critically the bone marrow involvement has to be minimal, less than ten percent of total nucleated cells, with negative MIBG or other imaging studies. This distinction matters because Stage 4-S, despite having metastatic disease, often has a favorable prognosis and can spontaneously regress.
keypoints: INRG L1: locoregional tumor, no image-defined risk factors
INRG L2: locoregional tumor with one or more image-defined risk factors
INRG M: distant metastatic disease (except MS)
INRG MS: L1/L2 tumor with mets confined to skin, liver, and/or marrow
INSS Stage 4S: age under 1, localized primary, marrow involvement under 10%
keypoint_voiceover: Know the four INRG stages, L one is locoregional without risk factors, L two is locoregional with image-defined risk factors, M is distant metastatic disease, and M-S is L one or L two with spread limited to skin, liver, or marrow. Separately, classic Stage 4-S requires age under one year, a localized primary tumor, and minimal marrow involvement under ten percent.
